title: Creating and Managing Threads
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of creating and managing threads in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply creating and managing threads in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to thread lifetime and cleanup and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Creating and Managing Threads through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding creating and managing threads helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Creating and Managing Threads helps you reason about starting and joining threads. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Starting and joining threads. Then connect it to Thread results and exceptions. The remaining syllabus points—Thread lifetime and cleanup—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Example: Creating and Managing Threads
content_blocks.code:
queue = Queue.new
worker = Thread.new { queue << "finished" }
puts queue.pop
worker.join

items.text: Test an empty value, a boundary value, and one invalid value before depending on the behavior.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports creating and managing threads. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for creating and managing threads using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Thread lifetime and cleanup), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Run, troubleshoot, and reset
content_blocks.text: Save as lesson.rb and run `ruby lesson.rb` from a terminal. CodeLeaf currently has no isolated Ruby runner, so these examples should be run locally until one is deployed. If the command fails, confirm `ruby --version`, inspect the full error message, and verify that required standard-library or gem dependencies are installed. Reset by removing temporary files created by your experiment and returning the code to the smallest reproducible example.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain creating and managing threads, identify its place in concurrency and asynchronous programming, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
